newsitem.title: USA: Blue-chips end record streak, bonds weaken.
newsitem.headline: Blue-chips end record streak, bonds weaken.

text.p: Blue-chip stocks ended slightly lower Monday as investors took profits after the market's eight-session stampede into record territory.
Bonds weakened as the market braced for upcoming supply. The dollar ended mixed.
The 30-share Dow Jones industrial average fell 1.12 points to 6,346.91, from Friday's record finish of 6,348.03.

"The market is actually taking a time-out. The broader market is no big deal and there's profit-taking in techs. The market is in a snooze mode," said Alfred Goldman, technical research director at A.G. Edwards & Co.
In the broader market, declining issues led advances 1,212 to 1,151 on active volume of 388 million shares on the New York Stock Exchange.
Right up to the last few minutes, the 30-share Dow appeared set to notch its ninth consecutive record but rallies in Dow components International Business Machines Corp. and Boeing Co. faded.
The blue-chip index had soared more than 325 points over the past two weeks before Monday's small pullback.
Ken Tower, an analyst at UST Securities, said the longest string of record closes for the Dow average remains 13, which ended on Jan. 20, 1987.

The Dow had jumped as high as 6,376.35 in the afternoon, aided by further strength in IBM and Boeing. IBM ended up two at 147, but off its high of 150 after Morgan Stanley raised its 12-month price target to $170 from $145 previously.
The Nasdaq Composite index fell 7.23 points to 1,254.57.

In the bond market, the 30-year Treasury fell 3/32, or 93.75 cents on a $1,000 bond, raising its yield to 6.47 percent from 6.46 percent at Friday's close. Bond prices and yields move in opposite directions.

The dollar rose to 111.53 yen late in New York from 111.07 late Friday. The dollar fell to 1.5020 marks from 1.5093 marks, hurt mainly by wire service reports that a council member of the Bundesbank, Germany's central bank, said he saw no reason for the dollar to appreciate at this time.
Oil prices fell as two refineries came back on line after maintenance. At the New York Mercantile Exchange, December unleaded gasoline fell 1.15 cents to 65.77 cents a gallon.
December heating oil fell 0.76 cent at 71.85 cents a gallon. December crude fell 29 cents to $23.88 a barrel.

Soybean futures jumped after the Agriculture Department's weekly report showed export inspections set a record. November soybeans closed up 12-1/4 cents at $7.11-1/4 at bushel at the Chicago Board of Trade.
December wheat fell 3-1/4 cents to $3.94 a bushel at the CBOT, and traders noted that prices had fallen on Friday on the likelihood that Egypt might buy non-U.S. wheat.
Overseas, London's FTSE 100 index managed to rise 3.9 points to close at 3,962.1. In Tokyo, the key Nikkei 225 average closed down 133.36 points or 0.64 percent at 20,796.37.
